episodes.title: A Money Bill and a Financial Bill are not the same thing
sources: Constitution of India, Article 109 (special procedure for Money Bills: not introduced in the Council of States; 14 days; recommendations only)
Constitution of India, Article 110 (definition: 'only provisions dealing with' the listed matters; Speaker's decision final, 110(3); Speaker's certificate, 110(4))
Constitution of India, Article 117 (Financial Bills: President's recommendation; not introduced in the Council of States; 117(3) expenditure bills)
Constitution of India, Article 107(2) (a bill is passed only when agreed to by both Houses, subject to Articles 108 and 109)

quiz.q: What can the Rajya Sabha do with a Money Bill?
options: Reject it outright
Amend it, and the change is binding
Recommend changes within 14 days
Send it to a joint sitting
quiz.why: Right. Under Article 109 the Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days with recommendations, which the Lok Sabha may accept or reject.

review.note: Seed premise holds. Script states only what Articles 107, 109, 110 and 117 say. Article 117(3) expenditure bills (which can start in either House) and the joint sitting route (Art. 108) for Financial Bills are left out for length; 'can't start in the Rajya Sabha' applies to 117(1) bills only, which the line refers to. Supreme Court cases on the Speaker's certificate (e.g. Aadhaar, Rojer Mathew) deliberately omitted per the brief. Art. 107(2) was not fetched as text; check it. Not verified against a primary source: Article 110(1): a Bill is a Money Bill if it contains only provisions dealing with matters such as taxes, government borrowing, and the custody of / appropriation from the Consolidated Fund; Article 110(3): the Speaker's decision on whether a Bill is a Money Bill is final; 110(4): the Speaker's certificate is endorsed on it; Article 109: a Money Bill is not introduced in the Council of States; the Council returns it within 14 days with recommendations; the Lok Sabha may accept or reject all or any of them; Article 117(1): a Bill making provision for any of the matters in Art. 110(1)(a)-(f) needs the President's recommendation and shall not be introduced in the Council of States; a bill that also has other provisions is therefore not a Money Bill (110(1) 'only'); After introduction, a Financial Bill follows the ordinary procedure: it is passed only when both Houses agree (Art. 107(2)); the Rajya Sabha's 14-day limit does not apply. episodes.title: An ordinance can't be renewed forever
sources: Constitution of India, Article 123 (President's ordinances during recess; 123(2)(a): laid before both Houses, cease six weeks from reassembly or earlier on disapproval by both Houses)
Constitution of India, Article 213 (Governor's ordinances; parallel provision)
Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar, Supreme Court, seven-judge Constitution Bench, judgment of 2 January 2017 (majority by Chandrachud J.; Lokur J. dissenting in part; Thakur CJI separate)

quiz.q: What did Krishna Kumar Singh hold about re-promulgation?
options: It is a fraud on the Constitution
It is allowed up to three times
It needs Rajya Sabha approval
It is beyond judicial review
quiz.why: Right. The seven-judge bench held in 2017 that re-promulgating ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution and a subversion of democratic legislative processes.

review.note: Seed premise holds. The case concerned Governor's ordinances in Bihar (Art. 213); the Court's reasoning covers Arts. 123 and 213, and the video's Article 123 line is the constitutional text, not the case. Nuances omitted: Lokur J. held laying to be directory; Thakur CJI left the laying question open; the holding on rights surviving an expired ordinance; D.C. Wadhwa (1987). The judgment text itself was not fetched (summaries from SC Observer and LiveLaw only); check the holdings against the judgment. Quiz phrase 'fraud on the Constitution' should be checked against the judgment wording. Not verified against a primary source: Article 123(1): the President may promulgate ordinances except when both Houses of Parliament are in session (i.e. during recess); Article 123(2)(a): an ordinance shall be laid before both Houses and ceases at the expiration of six weeks from the reassembly of Parliament, or earlier if both Houses pass resolutions disapproving it; Krishna Kumar Singh v. episodes.title: Dissolving the Lok Sabha kills some bills, not all
sources: Constitution of India, Article 107(3), (4), (5): prorogation; bills pending in the Council of States not passed by the House of the People; bills that lapse on dissolution
Constitution of India, Article 108(1) and (5): joint sitting; a joint sitting may be held notwithstanding an intervening dissolution once the President has notified it

quiz.q: Which bill does not lapse when the Lok Sabha is dissolved?
options: A bill pending in the Lok Sabha
Passed by Lok Sabha, pending in Rajya Sabha
Pending in Rajya Sabha, not passed by LS
A Rajya Sabha bill now in the Lok Sabha
quiz.why: Right. Under Article 107(4), a bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha has not passed does not lapse on dissolution.

review.note: Seed premise holds. All rules are from the text of Articles 107 and 108. Omitted: the Rajya Sabha itself is never dissolved; assurances, motions and resolutions also lapse under the Rules of Procedure (not in the Constitution); bills passed by both Houses awaiting assent do not lapse (practice and Article 111, not stated in 107). The closing line is a memory aid, not a legal test. Not verified against a primary source: Article 107(5): a bill pending in the House of the People, or passed by it and pending in the Council of States, lapses on dissolution, subject to Article 108; Article 107(4): a bill pending in the Council of States which has not been passed by the House of the People does not lapse on dissolution; Article 108(5): once the President has notified a joint sitting, it may be held and the bill passed notwithstanding an intervening dissolution; Article 107(3): a bill pending in Parliament does not lapse by reason of prorogation. episodes.title: Parliament can amend almost anything, but not the Constitution's identity
sources: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, Supreme Court, 13-judge bench, judgment of 24 April 1973 (7:6)
